Instructional leadership and student achievement in a centrally regulated system: A school-level test of academic optimism as an organisational pathway
abstract: This study examines how instructional leadership is associated with school-level student achievement within a centrally regulated education system, positioning academic optimism as a key organisational mediator. Rooted in the indirect-effects perspective, the study investigates whether leadership relates to student outcomes by shaping a collective belief system defined by academic emphasis, collective efficacy, and trust. Data were collected from 934 teachers across 205 Anatolian high schools in Türkiye and merged with official achievement records for 41,847 tenth-grade students. School-level structural equation modelling, controlling for family socioeconomic status, reveals a theoretically anticipated competitive mediation pattern. Instructional leadership shows a statistically significant positive indirect association with achievement through academic optimism, while its residual direct association with achievement is negative. These results suggest a dual process in centralised high-stakes accountability contexts: principals indirectly promote achievement by cultivating an optimistic academic culture, whereas the negative direct path reflects supervisory escalation in response t

title: Only for school heroes? A qualitative study of Argentine school principals under structural constraints
abstract: This article examines school leadership under structural constraints in Argentina. Drawing primarily on 128 semistructured interviews with primary and secondary principals, and using regulatory analysis and official statistics for contextual triangulation, it analyzes how principals lead when distributed leadership is limited by hierarchical governance, concentrated accountability, weak inter-institutional support, scarce organizational time, and fragile collaborative structures. The findings show hybrid configurations in which collaboration, informal teacher leadership, and relational support coexist with individualized responsibility and institutional solitude. The article distinguishes educational infrastructure, understood as the broader institutional environment of leadership, from structural constraints, understood as restrictive conditions experienced by principals as relatively fixed limits on action. It argues that heroic leadership is not an individual trait or moral exception, but a structural effect of systems that depend on principals to compensate for regulatory, organizational, and relational deficits.

title: School leaders’ crisis management responsibilities in the shadows of safety: A content analysis of educational leadership standards across the United States
abstract: School leaders are expected to prepare for, respond to, and lead recovery efforts after a crisis that disrupts the normal operation of schools. However, empirical evidence suggests that principals may be unprepared to fulfill these responsibilities. Given the influence of standards on what principals learn and are expected to know, this study examines the educational leadership standards for 49 states and the District of Columbia to understand the extent to which, and how, they frame school leaders’ crisis management expectations. Through summative content analysis, we find minimal attention to these functions, with only 10 states explicitly referencing crisis or crisis management. A second key finding is the predominant framing of crisis management as ensuring school safety, with an emphasis on physical safety. We offer implications for discussions about principals’ crisis management responsibilities for consideration in future revisions of national and state standards. We also highlight implications for preparation programs, emphasizing the need for curricula that address required crisis management functions and competencies.

title: Student-centered leadership in higher education: Perspectives from academic Department Heads
abstract: Student engagement, learning outcomes, and competency development have garnered growing attention in higher education. However, academic leaders often face challenges in fostering holistic student learning while also enhancing student career prospects. Drawing on student-centered leadership (SCL) theory, this study examines how university Department Heads (DHs) facilitate student learning and development, and explores the extent to which the K-12 SCL model is transferable to higher education contexts. The case study draws on semistructured interviews with eight DHs in a Canadian university. Data were analyzed using abductive reasoning. Findings show that DHs acted as operational actors who sought to improve learning outcomes by integrating high-impact practices into, and enhancing the quality of, teaching and curricula. A deep analysis of the findings suggests that DHs were required to make trade-offs between administrative compliance and student-centered practices, as their professional agency was constrained by intersecting cultural, structural, and resource-related factors. title: Should I stay or should I go? Quantitative analysis of school leaders’ intentions to transfer or exit through the lens of the job demands–resources model
abstract: This study investigated the differential effects of school leaders’ intention to leave the school (transfer) or the profession (exit) using the job demands–resources model as a theoretical lens. Working overtime and the socioeconomic status of the school were considered job demands, while psychological safety was regarded as a job resource, and self-efficacy was categorized as a personal resource. Structural equation modeling was performed on a sample of 956 school leaders with transfer intentions and 2179 school leaders with exit intentions from across Switzerland. The analysis revealed that job demands were not significant predictors of transfer or exit intentions, or job satisfaction. However, psychological safety had a significant, direct and negative effect on transfer and exit intentions, as well as a significant indirect effect via job satisfaction. Self-efficacy not only had a significant indirect effect via job satisfaction on both intentions, but also a significant, direct and positive effect on transfer intentions. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of focusing on strengthening job resources rather than reducing job demands in the context of turnover of schoo

title: The mediating role of adaptive expertise in the relationship between transformational leadership and teacher collaborative professionalism in Tanzanian schools
abstract: This mixed-methods study explores whether adaptive expertise mediates the relationship between transformational leadership and teacher collaborative professionalism in Tanzanian secondary schools – a resource-constrained context where imported leadership models often produce disappointing results. Surveying 439 teachers across 15 schools, with follow-up principal interviews, the study uses structural equation modelling and multi-group analysis. Adaptive expertise does mediate the leadership–collaboration link, but only through two of its four dimensions. Knowledge and innovation serve as positive pathways: when principals build teachers’ shared knowledge and encourage collaborative innovation, teachers report greater collaboration. In contrast, metacognition (reflective thinking) remains a private activity that does not translate into collaborative practice, and autonomy (freedom to act) benefits only teachers with master's degrees, not the majority. The direct effect of transformational leadership on collaboration is negative, suggesting that inspirational rhetoric without material support and follow-through may actually trigger teacher disengagement. title: How does principals’ job crafting relate to leadership for learning? Emotional regulation as a mediating mechanism in a centralised education system
abstract: This study examines how principals’ job crafting relates to leadership for learning through emotional regulation. Although leadership for learning is central to school improvement, limited attention has been paid to the proactive work-design behaviours that support its implementation. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, we propose that principals who actively craft their jobs by increasing structural resources and seeking challenging demands are better able to regulate their emotions, which may support their capacity to enact leadership for learning (LfL) practices. Using survey data from 698 principals working in K-12 schools across 14 provinces in Türkiye, we employed latent structural equation modelling to test direct and indirect relationships. The findings indicated that principal job crafting is positively related to LfL and that emotional regulation partially mediates this relationship. title: Teacher leadership and school improvement in Asia: A systematic review
abstract: This systematic review synthesizes 74 empirical studies to examine the role of teacher leadership in school improvement across Asian contexts. Teacher leadership is conceptualized as a dynamic, relational process through which teachers influence colleagues and school culture to support instructional improvement. Following PRISMA guidelines, the review identifies three core dimensions: leadership enactment, enabling organizational conditions and school improvement outcomes and proposes a conceptual model of their interaction. The findings indicate that professional growth and change agency are the most frequently reported outcomes while principal support is a key enabling condition for teacher leadership. The review further highlights that teacher leadership in Asian contexts is shaped by cultural values such as collective harmony and relational trust. However, the evidence reveals a lack of longitudinal research and a need for culturally attuned leadership models that reflect Asian educational contexts. These findings provide a strategic roadmap for policymakers and practitioners to institutionalize leadership pathways, strengthen professional learning communities and foster collab

title: Distributed leadership of middle leaders in a Singapore polytechnic
abstract: Despite growing studies on distributed leadership, significant gaps persist in understanding how it manifests in higher education, particularly within Asian hierarchical institutional settings. Limited research has examined middle leaders’ lived experiences in enacting distributed leadership. This study examines distributed leadership practices of middle leaders in a Singapore polytechnic, exploring their perceived experiences, affordances, and constraints within a higher education setting. Using phenomenological methodology, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 Course Leaders. Findings revealed that middle leaders enacted distributed leadership through informal role assignments based on expertise, networking with stakeholders to create leadership development opportunities, facilitating shared decision-making, and fostering collective engagement. Key affordances included domain knowledge proficiency, stakeholder relationships, and operational familiarity, whilst key constraints encompassed inadequate leadership preparation, complex stakeholder management and administrative burdens. title: Relational infrastructure and distributed leadership: A longitudinal study of school system development
abstract: Distributed leadership in schools has attracted substantial research attention, yet how the organizational conditions it requires actually develop over time remains poorly understood. This article addresses that question through a 3-year longitudinal study of school system development in a Swedish municipality, engaging principals, deputy principals, and middle leaders across an entire school system in sustained collective work. We introduce the concept of relational infrastructure—the trust networks, dialogue practices, and shared meaning-making processes that enable collaborative leadership to emerge and endure—and propose a four-phase process model showing how these conditions develop from individual experimentation to organizational culture. Relational infrastructure extends the educational infrastructure perspective by theorizing relational and cultural dimensions that existing frameworks identify but do not fully develop. The study contributes a processual account of distributed leadership development at system level, showing how relational infrastructure is built through deliberate developmental work within a stable formal architecture, how it deepens across phases, and how

title: Coping under fire: Street-level school leadership in wartime
abstract: During prolonged wartime conditions, school principals must lead their communities while mediating pressures from multiple stakeholders, allocating scarce resources, and interpreting ambiguous policy goals under ongoing uncertainty. This study examines how principals cope with the challenges they face during prolonged wartime conditions. Drawing on the street-level bureaucracy framework and Tummers and colleagues’ typology of coping among public professionals, we conceptualize coping as a relational and discretionary process through which principals continuously negotiate competing institutional and emotional demands. Using 60 semistructured, in-depth interviews with Israeli school principals in the wake of October 7, 2023 and the ensuing war, we identify four coping movements: moving toward stakeholders, moving away from stakeholders, moving against stakeholders, and dynamically shifting between stakeholders. The findings demonstrate that coping under prolonged wartime conditions is not a stable or isolated response to external pressures, but rather a fluid, multidirectional, and politically embedded process that emerges through interactions with diverse stakeholders. title: Principal leadership styles and school violence: The mediating role of teachers’ professional commitment in Israeli Arab schools
abstract: School violence is shaped not only by student behavior but also by broader social dynamics and school level conditions, making leadership, and teacher-related factors especially important for understanding safer school climates. This study examines the direct and indirect associations (via teachers’ professional commitment) of transformational and transactional leadership with school violence. To reduce common method bias, data were collected from two sources: 213 senior management team members (SMT) and 213 teachers who were not SMT members, drawn from 71 middle and high schools in the Arab educational system in Israel. Data was aggregated at the school level of analysis. Structural equation modeling and bootstrapping analysis indicated that teachers’ professional commitment functions as a mediating mechanism linking both leadership styles to school violence. Higher professional commitment appears to enhance the effectiveness of principals’ leadership practices, supporting stronger leadership processes at the school level and contributing to a safer, more positive learning climate. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

title: Not all stressors are equal: Using ecological theory to examine systems that predict stress and mental health in principals
abstract: Stressors in the principalship are plentiful, but few studies have examined their differential impacts on work-stress and mental health, particularly from a systems perspective. Guided by Lazarus and Folkman's occupational stress theory and Bronfenbrenner's ecological theory, we conducted an embedded mixed-method design with a quantitative-dominant crossover analysis for hierarchical regression to identify emergent stressors, the systems from which they originate, and whether stressor systems, cumulatively and differentially, predict negative psychological outcomes including work-stress, anxiety, and depression. We identified ten thematic stressors that were organized into five systems based on proximity to the principalship and degree of control: nanosystem, microsystem, macrosystem, exosystem, and chronosystem. In our sample, principals reported high work-stress, moderate anxiety, and mild to moderate depression symptoms. Regression analyses showed that the cumulative number of stressors significantly predict work-stress. However, only system-level stressors, especially nanosystem stressors, predicted anxiety, and depression symptoms. Our study suggests that the amount of stresso

title: Enacting subject leadership as practice: Primary science and curriculum marginalisation in English primary schools
abstract: Subject leadership in primary schools is increasingly recognised as important for curriculum quality, yet little is known about how subject leadership is enacted as practice in marginalised curriculum areas such as science within high-accountability systems. This study explores how primary science subject leaders in English schools understand and enact their leadership role within a high-stakes accountability context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with science subject leaders across school contexts, the study adopts a leadership-as-practice and sensemaking theoretical lens to examine leadership as situated, relational, and shaped by organisational and policy conditions. Findings indicate that science leadership is enacted primarily through influence rather than formal authority, with leaders engaging in advocacy, relationship-building and ongoing negotiation to secure time, status and legitimacy for science within a crowded curriculum. Participants’ leadership practices were shaped by accountability pressures and the prioritisation of English and Mathematics, requiring leaders to respond creatively to inspection signals while sustaining teacher confidence and curriculum coh

title: Leadership development of university teachers in China: A mixed-methods model development and validation study
abstract: This study develops and validates a contextually grounded model of teacher leadership in Chinese higher education, addressing a gap in the literature dominated by school-based and Western-centric frameworks. Drawing on mixed methods, including grounded theory and confirmatory factor analysis, data were collected from 352 university faculty members across multiple Chinese provinces. This study employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design: (1) a qualitative phase (in-depth interviews) to generate context-specific dimensions and indicators of teacher leadership; and (2) a quantitative phase (survey) to test the emergent model via exploratory factor analysis/confirmatory factor analysis. The qualitative phase was conducted in October–November 2023; the quantitative survey took place from November 2023 to February 2024. The resulting four-dimensional model encompasses moral leadership, teaching leadership, research leadership, and team leadership. Findings reveal that moral and teaching leadership dominate faculty perceptions, reflecting the cultural importance of ethical conduct and pedagogical engagement in the Chinese academic tradition. title: The enduring popularity of distributed leadership: Professional participation or task allocation?
Mediating ambiguity: Principals’ sense-making and instructional leadership in curriculum reform enactment
abstract: Effective leadership by school principals is reported to involve shaping school cultures, fostering collaboration, allocating resources, and motivating teachers’ attitudes which results in (in-)directly impacting student learning. While the literature recommends a move toward collective and distributed processes of sense-making, the role of the school principal and their respective leadership practices in the context of curriculum reform is still largely underrepresented. Using an integrated framework of policy enactment, sense-making and instructional leadership, this article explores how school principals interpreted curriculum reform at lower secondary level in the Republic of Ireland and how these interpretations translated into leadership practices. This qualitative study, part of a larger national 4-year longitudinal study, interviewed 65 secondary school principals approximately a decade after implementation regarding their experiences of leading Junior Cycle reforms. Our findings reveal that in contested reform contexts, instructional leadership dimensions of programme management and climate-building functionally collapse into reciprocal practices shaped by principals’ diag

title: Governing teacher well-being in international policy discourse: Problem representation, accountability, and the individualisation of care
abstract: Teacher well-being has become a prominent concern in contemporary education policy, yet it is rarely treated as a structural or ethical responsibility in its own right. Instead, it is frequently mobilised instrumentally through its assumed effects on performance, retention, and system efficiency. This article examines how teacher well-being is constituted as a policy problem within internationally circulating education policy discourse. Drawing on Bacchi’s What's the Problem Represented to be? (WPR) approach, and informed by White's relational conceptualisation of well-being, it develops an interpretive policy analysis of influential texts through which it is made visible and governed across contexts. The analysis shows that well-being is predominantly represented as an individual responsibility, to be secured through resilience, self-regulation, and emotional self-management, rather than as a condition shaped by organisational and material arrangements. This framing is reinforced through governance technologies, including accountability frameworks, performance metrics, and well-being agendas, which render it governable as an individual attribute while redistributing responsibility

title: Meso-level education governance: The rise and fall of regional improvement collaboratives in Scotland
abstract: Academic research has increasingly prioritised learner-centred reform, often overlooking the political dynamics that shape how reforms unfold. Large-scale change frequently falters because technocratic approaches fail to account for these complex political processes, while neoliberal, performance-driven agendas reinforce top-down reforms that marginalise the cultural and relational dimensions essential for meaningful improvement. This article examines the politics of education reform in Scotland through the creation and dissolution of the Regional Improvement Collaboratives (RICs), established after the 2016 Governance Review. Although the Review aimed to develop a more empowered, school-led system grounded in subsidiarity, the RICs exposed persistent tensions between local autonomy and central oversight and highlighted the dominance of structural over cultural change. Documentary analysis shows how policy narratives shaped governance and practice, revealing challenges in collaboration, the limiting effects of restricted funding and the impact of uneven evaluation and shifting national priorities. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that efforts to empower the system were undermined

title: From heroic leadership myth to street-level management: School principals’ experiences of sensemaking and creative insubordination under incomplete autonomy
abstract: The normative ‘heroic leadership’ discourse positions school principals as transformative visionaries, yet in highly centralised systems this narrative breaks down, giving rise to the twin challenges of ‘incomplete autonomy’ and ‘street-level management’. This phenomenological study examines how 15 principals in Türkiye's centralised education system respond to structural disempowerment: how they make sense of authority gaps and develop creative insubordination practices to keep their schools running. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenological reduction. Three themes emerged: (1) Structural Siege and the Experience of Incomplete Autonomy, (2) Sensemaking and Creative Insubordination Under the Grip of Incomplete Autonomy, and (3) Lack of Psychological Safety and the Bureaucratic Vice. Principals are not passive implementers; when rigid regulations clash with urgent educational needs, they act – moving along a continuum from legitimate discretion to creative insubordination – to prevent schools from grinding to a halt.
